A: Axial T2WI of an 8-year-old girl with MELAS showing posterior-predominant cortical/subcortical hyperintensities crossing vascular territories, a textbook stroke-like lesion. B: Axial T2FLAIR of the same MELAS patient showing the same cortical/subcortical stroke-like hyperintensities; classic bright thickened cortical band described in the text. C: Post-contrast T1WI of the MELAS patient showing linear enhancement of the left cortical stroke-like lesion, a recognized feature of acute stroke-like episodes. E: DWI of the MELAS patient showing gyriform hyperintensity in the stroke-like lesion area, a classic acute-phase finding. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Real human axial brain FLAIR T2-w MRI of a MELAS patient (28-year-old, 3243A>G mutation) showing cortical-subcortical temporo-parieto-occipital stroke-like lesions, a specific manifestation of MELAS. B: Real human axial brain FLAIR T2-w MRI of a MELAS patient (59-year-old female, T10191C ND3 mutation) showing parieto-occipital cortical/juxtacortical stroke-like lesion with the recognized 'black toenails' sign, a specific MELAS manifestation. C: Real human axial brain FLAIR T2-w MRI of a MELAS patient (30-year-old male, T3271C mtDNA mutation) showing a chronic parieto-occipital stroke-like lesion with volume loss and cavitary necrosis, a specific MELAS manifestation.

panels.figure_caption: Conventional neuroimaging of three representative MELAS patients. (A) A 28‐year‐old patient harboring the 3243A > G/MT‐TLA1 mutation and presenting the typical features of stroke‐like lesions (SLL). Axial FLAIR T2‐w shows cortical‐subcortical lesions prevalently in the temporo‐parieto‐occipital regions. (B) A 59‐year‐old female with T10191C ND3 mutation (#15) was asymptomatic at MRI scan and had the last stroke‐like episode (SLE) more than 3 months previously. She presented occipital epilepsy from childhood with several episodes of status epilepticus. Axial FLAIR T2‐w showed gyral necrosis affecting the cortex and juxta cortical parieto‐occipital white matter with partial gyral signal suppression on T2/FLAIR sequences, a feature referred to as “black toenails” sign. (C) A 30‐year‐old male with T3271CmtDNA mutation (#19) was asymptomatic at scan evaluation. One month before the scan, he had an SLE that clinically presented with epileptic seizures. Axial FLAIR shows a chronic lesion with focal brain volume reduction in the right parieto‐occipital white matter, characterized by T2 FLAIR hyperintensity with secondary ventricular dilatation and foci of cavitary white matter necrosis.

panels.figure_caption: Polymorphism of lesions. Case 5, A 12-year-old boy with MELAS. (A) CT image. Density decreases in the left occipital lobe; calcification is slightly evident on the left (wide arrow). (B,C) MRI was performed after 3 days in the same boy. FLAIR (B) showed polymorphism of the lesion: Cortex swelling on the left occipital (red arrows) and cortex atrophy with gliosis (yellow arrow) on the right occipital. T1WI (C) showed hyperintensity in the bilateral basal ganglia and hypointensity in the left occipital region.
in_text_mentions: In this study, we propose the concept of lesion polymorphism, which refers to the spatial diversity of lesions in a single neuroimaging examination. Forty of 59 (68%) studies showed polymorphisms of lesions in our cohort, which might show cortex swelling, cortex atrophy with gliosis in different regions and calcification of the bilateral basal ganglia (Figure 4).

findings.label: Ragged-red fibers on muscle biopsy
findings.evidence: Caption: 'Gömöri trichrome preparation showing scattered ragged red fibres'; visual: several myofibers with red-purple subsarcolemmal accumulations against blue-green fibers; in-text: 'A subsequent skeletal muscle biopsy revealed ragged red fibres (Fig 2)' in a patient with A3243G mutation characteristic of MELAS syndrome

panels.rationale: Single-panel light-microscopy image of a human skeletal-muscle biopsy stained with Gömöri trichrome, visibly showing scattered fibers with red-purple subsarcolemmal accumulations (ragged-red fibers) against blue-green myofibers. The caption explicitly describes this finding, and the in-text attribution confirms it in a patient with genetically confirmed MELAS syndrome (A3243G mutation) within a disease-focused article. Ragged-red fibers are a classic histological manifestation of MELAS syndrome, so the panel is a real patient image showing a specific clinical manifestation of the configured target disease and qualifies for inclusion. [raw subtype: A3243G]

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial brain MRI (FLAIR left, DWI right) of a human patient from the MELAS (m.3243A>T) article. Multifocal cortical gray-matter FLAIR hyperintensities in right temporal/parietal/occipital lobes with left temporal white-matter lesions that explicitly do not follow vascular territories and lack restricted diffusion — the textbook MELAS stroke-like cortical lesion. Disease attribution (title) and manifestation (caption/in-text) are directly supported. B: Follow-up axial brain MRI after a documented stroke-like episode in the same MELAS patient, showing expansion to extended white-matter and left thalamic lesions. This represents evolution of the MELAS stroke-like lesion process directly tied by the caption/in-text to the disease; real human neuroimaging. The thalamic component is listed as a proposed finding because it is not covered by the vocabulary.

panels.figure_caption: Brain MRIs obtained 14 days after the onset of initial symptom. A brain MRI obtained on admission (day 1) shows increased DWI/FLAIR signal in the left anterolateral temporal lobe, mainly along the cortex with edema (a, b, arrows). The follow-up brain MRI obtained on day 28 shows a newly appearing increased DWI/FLAIR signal in the right anterior temporal lobe, and posterior spread of the initial left temporal lesion along the cerebral cortex (compatible with classic stroke-like lesion). Note mild reduction in ADC values in the left anterior temporal cortex (c, arrowhead), suggesting ongoing regional metabolic derangements. ADC values in the left anterior temporal subcortical white matter is rather increased, suggesting the presence of vasogenic edema. A: DWI; B: FLAIR; C: ADC map

A: Axial FLAIR MRI at the level of the lateral ventricles from the 3T MRI performed for a second stroke-like event in a MELAS patient (article: 'Microhemorrhages in MELAS Lesions: A Case Report'). Human patient neuroimaging showing the previously affected cortical area with near-normalized signal, part of the stroke-like lesion evolution. No printed panel letter; labels assigned by reading order of the 2x2 montage. B: Axial ADC map from the same 3T MRI session in a MELAS patient, demonstrating the diffusion correlate of the second stroke-like cortical lesion. Real human patient neuroimaging directly supporting the MELAS manifestation described in the caption. C: Susceptibility-weighted MRI with yellow inset box and magnified view showing small hypointense foci consistent with microhemorrhages, matching the caption 'microhemorrhages persisted'. Microhemorrhages are a recognized but less commonly emphasized (non-textbook) feature of MELAS...

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A1, A2, B). A1: Sagittal T1-weighted MRI showing high-signal intensity consistent with calcification of the right basal ganglia in a MELAS syndrome patient. Basal ganglia calcification is a recognized neuroimaging feature of MELAS. A2: Sagittal T1-weighted MRI showing high-signal intensity consistent with calcification of the left basal ganglia in a MELAS syndrome patient. Basal ganglia calcification is a recognized neuroimaging feature of MELAS. B: Axial DWI MRI showing high-signal intensity lesions consistent with lacunar infarcts in the left caudate nucleus and corona radiata. While MELAS typically presents with cortical stroke-like lesions crossing vascular territories, lacunar infarcts represent a variant cerebrovascular manifestation in this patient. The closest vocabulary finding is used.
